Detector.Details:
Detects double-checked locking pattern that is broken due to missing volatile keyword on the shared field.

Double-checked locking was broken in Java 1.4 and earlier. In Java 5+, it requires the shared field to be declared as volatile to work correctly.

BugPattern.LongDescription: {0} uses double-checked locking pattern but field {1} is not declared volatile. This can lead to partially constructed objects being published.
BugPattern.Details:
Problem

The double-checked locking pattern relies on the Java Memory Model's happens-before guarantees. Without the volatile keyword, another thread may see a partially constructed object due to instruction reordering.

Example


// Bad: Missing volatile
private static Singleton instance;  // ❌ Not volatile

public static Singleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {  // First check (no lock)
        synchronized (Singleton.class) {
            if (instance == null) {  // Second check (with lock)
                instance = new Singleton();  // ❌ Can publish partial object
            }
        }
    }
    return instance;
}

// Good: With volatile
private static volatile Singleton instance;  // ✅ Volatile

public static Singleton getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) {
        synchronized (Singleton.class) {
            if (instance == null) {
                instance = new Singleton();  // ✅ Safe publication
            }
        }
    }
    return instance;
}

// Better: Use initialization-on-demand holder idiom
private static class Holder {
    static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton();
}
public static Singleton getInstance() {
    return Holder.INSTANCE;  // Thread-safe lazy initialization
}

Solutions

  1. Add volatile keyword to the shared field
  2. Use initialization-on-demand holder idiom (preferred)
  3. Use eager initialization if lazy loading is not required
  4. Use enum singleton pattern (simplest and safest)

Why volatile is Required

Without volatile, the JVM may reorder the instructions:

  1. Allocate memory for Singleton
  2. Assign instance = memory address (before constructor completes!)
  3. Call constructor to initialize fields

Another thread may see instance != null but with uninitialized fields.

References

  • The "Double-Checked Locking is Broken" Declaration
  • Java Concurrency in Practice (Section 16.2.4)
